title: One thing at a time, badly.
dek: Five projects of 40 hours, 10 hours a week: done together, all of them finish at week 20. Done one by one, the average finishes at week 12, and at week 10 two are already done.
whyThisIdea: Este următoarea idee nefolosită din backlog (#20; am sărit din nou peste #1, #7 și #14, încă marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate). E duminică, ziua în care îți faci lista pentru săptămână, iar aritmetica (5 proiecte × 40 de ore, 10 ore pe săptămână) arată că aceleași ore, făcute pe rând, termină proiectul mediu cu 8 săptămâni mai devreme.

entry.title: One thing at a time, badly.
entry.titleHtml: One thing at a time, badly.
entry.dek: Five projects of 40 hours, 10 hours a week: done together, all of them finish at week 20. Done one by one, the average finishes at week 12, and at week 10 two are already done.
body: “Five things at 20% is not one thing at 100%. It is zero things, five times.”

Have you ever asked yourself how many things you have started this year and how many of them you have actually finished? Today is Sunday, the 15th of November, and Sunday is the day I usually make plans for the week. And if you are a student like me, the list probably looks something like this: a course you started, a side project, the gym, a book on the desk, a language app. Everything is “in progress”. Nothing is done. So the question is: is doing five things a little bit every week really better than doing one thing properly, even badly? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is the habit of running many projects at the same time, and I met it in my own week, not in a book. It feels very responsible. Every project gets a little bit of attention, none of them is abandoned, and when somebody asks “how is it going?”, you can say “good, I am working on it” about all of them. That is exactly the part that made me suspicious, because it is a sentence that can be true forever.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “One thing at a time” and “badly”. The first half is about order - not doing less, but doing the same things one after another instead of all together. The second half is the one that is harder to accept. When you have only one project, you look at it every day, and every day you see how bad it is. With five projects, you never have to look at any of them for too long, so none of them has to be bad yet. <u>Five open projects are a very comfortable place to hide from the quality of each one.</u> Doing one thing badly means finishing it and letting people see it, and that is scarier than keeping five things safe at 20%.

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic, because this is where it surprised me. Let’s say I have 5 projects, each one needs about 40 hours to be finished, and I have 10 hours a week for them. These numbers are my assumptions, not a measurement. Done all together, every project gets 2 hours a week:
40 hours ÷ 2 hours a week = week 20 for every single project
Done one after another, every project gets the full 10 hours:
40 hours ÷ 10 hours a week = 4 weeks each, so they finish at weeks 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20

Look at the last number. The fifth project finishes at week 20 in both cases. So I lose nothing at the end - the total work is exactly the same, 200 hours. But the average project is finished at week 12 instead of week 20, eight weeks earlier. And now let’s stop the clock in the middle, at week 10. Done all together, I have five projects at 50% and zero finished. Done one after another, I have two finished and the third one half done. Same hours, same effort, and at week 10 one version of me has two things to show and the other has nothing.

And this is in the perfect case, where changing from one project to another costs nothing. In real life it costs something every time - you need to remember where you stopped, open the right files, get back into the idea. I wrote about this in my article about the phone, so I will not repeat it, but the point is that every cost of switching makes the parallel version even worse, never better. The order is free. The switching is not.

There is also a reason why the half is worth so little. A course you did 50% of does not give you half of a certificate. A blog post that is half written is not half published - nobody can read it. A project at 80% is, for everybody except you, the same as a project that does not exist. <u>Most things pay only when they are finished, not for every hour you put in.</u> That is why the finished ones matter so much more than the percentage on the list.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Not everything can be done one at a time. School is the obvious example - I cannot study only maths for four weeks and then only history, because the exams are all in the same session. And for learning itself, there is research on the other side. In 2007, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor published a study with a very honest title: “The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning”. Students who practised different types of problems mixed together did better on a later test than the ones who practised one type at a time. So mixing is not always wrong. But I think there is a difference between mixing exercises inside one subject and keeping five different projects open for months. The first one is a way of learning. The second one, at least for me, is a way of never finishing.

So here is what I am going to try, starting today, because it is Sunday and the list is in front of me. From all the things that are “in progress”, I pick one, the closest to being done, and it gets most of my free hours until it is finished - finished, not perfect. The others are not deleted, they wait in a list with a date. This blog is actually the proof for me that it works. In my article about Atomic Habits I wrote that I did not start anything until somebody asked me “So what did you write?”. The first post was one book, written once, not five ideas kept open.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most of my “in progress” is just a nicer word for “not done”, and that one thing finished badly teaches me more than five things kept at 20%. But I have to be honest about two things. My arithmetic assumes that every project is equally important and equally long, and real life is never that clean. And sometimes a project is blocked - you are waiting for someone, or the idea needs time - and then having a second thing to work on is not hiding, it is just common sense. What I take from it is smaller: before starting something new, ask what you could finish instead.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Five things at 20% is not one thing at 100%. It is zero things, five times.”
